claim_text: Markdown became an increasingly restrictive output format as agents grew more powerful, and members of the Claude Code team now prefer HTML for outputs they read, share, and use as specs and reference files
evidence_span: Instead, I've started preferring HTML as an output format instead of Markdown and increasingly see this pattern being applied by others on the Claude Code team.

claim_text: A Markdown file past roughly a hundred lines stops actually being read — by its author and still less by anyone else in the organization — while an HTML document stays navigable because Claude can structure it visually with tabs, illustrations, and links
evidence_span: But HTML documents are much easier to read because Claude can organize the structure visually to be ideal to navigate with tabs, illustrations, and links.

claim_text: HTML can represent tabular data, design data in CSS, SVG illustrations, code, interactions, workflows, spatial data, and images, so almost nothing Claude can read cannot be efficiently represented in it — and without that reach the model falls back on inefficient Markdown substitutes like ASCII diagrams or estimating colors with unicode characters
evidence_span: the model may do more inefficient things in Markdown, like ASCII diagrams or, my favorite, estimating colors with unicode characters

claim_text: Markdown is hard to share because most browsers do not render it natively, so it travels as an email attachment, whereas an uploaded HTML file shares as a link — and the chance of someone actually reading a spec, report, or PR writeup is much higher in HTML
evidence_span: Markdown files are fairly hard to share since most browsers do not render them natively well.

claim_text: A throwaway HTML editor built for one piece of data works because it ends with an export — a copy-as-JSON or copy-as-prompt button turning what was done in the UI back into something pasteable into Claude Code — which keeps the human in the loop while tightening it
evidence_span: You stay in the loop, but the loop gets much tighter.

claim_text: Planning in HTML replaces the single plan file with a web of files for different stages — explorations, mockups, then the implementation plan — kept around as references, and the verification agent reading them in gains much broader context on what is needed
evidence_span: When verifying I'll also ask the verification agent to read in the files and it will have much broader context on what is needed.

claim_text: Markdown often uses fewer tokens, but HTML's added expressiveness and the much higher likelihood of the human actually reading it produce better output overall — a trade that a large context window makes barely noticeable
evidence_span: While Markdown often uses fewer tokens, I've found that the added expressiveness of HTML and the much higher likelihood of me reading it means I get overall better output.
